title: “I AM THE GOOD SHEPHERD”: THE OLD TESTAMENT PASSAGE THAT MAKES JESUS’ WORDS ALMOST TERRIFYINGLY BOLD
paragraphs: “I AM THE GOOD SHEPHERD”: THE OLD TESTAMENT PASSAGE THAT MAKES JESUS’ WORDS ALMOST TERRIFYINGLY BOLD

Jesus was not merely saying He cared about sheep. Ezekiel 34 had already declared that God Himself would come looking for His scattered flock. So when Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd,” the question was far bigger than most of us realize: Who, exactly, was standing before them?
There are sentences in the Bible that sound gentle only because we have heard them too many times.
“I am the good shepherd” is one of them.
Print it beneath paintings of Jesus carrying a lamb.
And none of that is wrong.
But familiarity can quietly remove the thunder from words that originally shook the ground.
And He certainly was not inventing a beautiful pastoral metaphor out of nowhere.
There was an ancient accusation hanging behind those words.
And then came a promise so staggering that centuries later, when Jesus opened His mouth in John 10, anyone soaked in Israel’s Scriptures had reason to feel the weight of what He was saying.
To understand why, you have to go backward.
And once you see what is there, “I am the good shepherd” may never sound tame again.
God speaks through Ezekiel against the shepherds of Israel.
The Hebrew word is רֹעִים — ro‘im — “shepherds,” from the verb רעה (ra‘ah), to shepherd, tend, or pasture.
But these shepherds were not caring for the flock.
“You eat the fat, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat ones, but you do not feed the sheep.”
Then comes an indictment that sounds painfully modern.
“The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought.”
Instead, God says, they ruled the flock “with force and harshness.”
That is the scandal of Ezekiel 34.
People entrusted with the sheep were using the sheep.
And perhaps that is where this ancient chapter stops feeling ancient.
Because some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to be wounded by somebody who was supposed to protect you.
Maybe your wound did not come from an obvious enemy.
Maybe it came from someone carrying a Bible.
Maybe from someone who could quote Scripture while manipulating you.
Maybe from a church leader whose public holiness concealed private cruelty.
Maybe from a Christian parent who taught grace but made home feel like judgment.
Maybe from someone who told you to forgive while refusing to repent.
Not necessarily because you stopped believing God existed.
Sometimes wounded sheep wander because they no longer know whom they can trust.
Ezekiel 34 does not minimize abusive shepherding to protect religious reputations.
But here is where the chapter becomes astonishing.
God does not merely announce that He will replace bad shepherds with better management.
“Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep.”
God says He is coming after His sheep.
So God Himself declares that He will shepherd His people.
Because centuries later Jesus stands in Israel and says:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός.
Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos.
The Greek adjective καλός (kalos) can carry the sense of good, noble, beautiful, excellent, worthy—the shepherd who is everything a shepherd ought to be.
But the force of John 10 becomes even richer when heard against Israel’s Scriptures.
Ezekiel had announced that God Himself would search for His sheep.
Ezekiel describes God rescuing His scattered flock.
Jesus says His sheep hear His voice.
Ezekiel promises that God will gather His sheep.
Jesus speaks of gathering His sheep into one flock.
Ezekiel condemns shepherds who consume the flock for themselves.
“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
False shepherds sacrifice the sheep to save themselves.
Jesus sacrifices Himself to save the sheep.
False shepherds sacrifice the sheep to save themselves.
Jesus sacrifices Himself to save the sheep.
And this is where Christianity stops being merely a philosophy about becoming a better person.
The Shepherd came for His sheep.
Not because the sheep had successfully found their own way home.
Isaiah had already described humanity this way:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way.”
We often reduce sin to a collection of especially ugly behaviors committed by especially terrible people.
Sin is humanity wandering from its Shepherd.
Our lives without rightful submission to the God who gave them.
Some become experts at looking close to the Shepherd while their hearts are miles away.
And maybe that last one is the most frightening.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still be lost.
You can sing worship songs while protecting a secret sin.
You can post Bible verses and quietly hate someone.
You can know how to say “God is good” while refusing to surrender the one room of your heart where you have hung a sign saying:
You can look clean enough to fool people.
But sheep do not save themselves by looking clean.
And Jesus did not say the good shepherd gives the sheep motivational advice.
“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
That sentence takes us toward a hill outside Jerusalem.
Toward the sinless Son of God willingly giving Himself for sinners.
Jesus says something remarkable in John 10:
“No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.”
The cross was not Jesus losing control of His mission.
The cross was central to His mission.
The Shepherd walked toward the wolves.
He placed Himself between judgment and His sheep.
The One without sin bore sin.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
And if you have spent years believing Christianity is essentially God telling bad people to behave better, look at the cross again.
Christianity begins with something far more devastating:
Grace does not pretend your wandering was harmless.
Grace tells the truth about how lost you were and then shows you how far the Shepherd was willing to go to bring sinners home.
Maybe you have wandered farther than anyone knows.
Maybe the version of you people see on Facebook is not the version of you that appears when the screen goes dark.
Maybe there are searches you delete.
Habits you keep promising to stop.
Maybe you have become skilled at saying “I’m okay” because explaining the truth feels exhausting.
Maybe you once burned for Christ.
At least you think you do.
And somewhere inside you is a frightening question:
Not merely the people who never made a public mess of their lives.
The ones who left the path.
The ones who made choices they regret.
The ones whose testimony contains chapters they wish they could tear out.
The ones whose story became a scandal.
And this is precisely where our theme becomes more than a slogan:
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming sin so repentance becomes unnecessary.
Jesus rewrites lives by confronting sin, forgiving repentant sinners, restoring the broken, and transforming those who come to Him.
Grace is not God saying your sin does not matter.
The cross proves it mattered terribly.
Grace is God providing in Christ what guilty sinners could never provide for themselves.
The Shepherd does not merely find us so we can continue wandering with religious reassurance.
He brings us under His shepherding.
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”
Real grace does not only comfort.
Jesus does not save us so sin can remain king with Christian decorations hanging around its throne.
And there may be something in your life right now that you already know the Shepherd has been confronting.
You do not need another sign.
A relationship pulling you away from Christ.
A wound you have turned into an excuse to wound others.
And remarkably, being fully known by Christ does not mean you are beyond His reach.
The terrifying beauty of the Gospel is that Christ knows what we desperately hope nobody discovers, yet He still calls sinners to come into the light, repent, believe, and follow Him.
Do not confuse that invitation with permission to remain unchanged.
The Shepherd who carries wounded sheep also leads them.
And sometimes following Him means finally admitting:
Maybe that is your prayer tonight.
Not because typing three words saves anyone.
But sometimes bringing our struggle into the light is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building.
There are believers reading beside you who understand what it means to limp behind the Shepherd.
Let somebody else who is drowning discover that grace still reaches people in deep water.
That person who stopped attending church.
That person who jokes about Christianity because getting serious about God would hurt too much.
That believer who seems strong but has been strangely quiet.

We cannot know whose screen this will appear on at 2:13 in the morning when temptation has won again, the marriage feels dead, shame is suffocating them, or they are wondering whether God could possibly want them back.
A share can become a doorway through which someone encounters Scripture.
Return to Ezekiel 34 and John 10 when you forget what kind of Shepherd Jesus is.
There is also a practical way to help this ministry continue producing and distributing Christ-centered resources.
Christ purchased redemption; we cannot purchase righteousness.
The Gospel does not need to be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
What matters eternally is whether you belong to the Shepherd.
Because Ezekiel 34 eventually contains another detail we cannot ignore.
After God promises, “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep,” He also promises:
“I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David.”
Ezekiel was writing long after the historical King David had lived.
The promise therefore looks forward—to the Davidic shepherd-king God would appoint over His people.
This is why the statement is explosive.
John 10 is not giving us a sentimental picture of a religious teacher who happens to be unusually compassionate.
Jesus stands inside Israel’s great shepherd promises and presents Himself as their fulfillment.
And the divine rescue promised in Ezekiel is coming into focus in Him.
Then John takes us even deeper.
His opponents understand enough of the claim that they pick up stones.
The Shepherd is not merely offering therapy for wounded sheep.
And offering His sheep eternal life.
So perhaps the most important question this article can leave with you is not:
Do I agree that Jesus is the Good Shepherd?
Because you can admire a shepherd without belonging to his flock.
And still refuse to follow Jesus personally.
Christ does not call us merely to admire Him.
Let Him expose what must be exposed.
Let Him forgive what you cannot undo.
Let Him heal what others broke.
Let Him remove what is destroying you.
Let Him lead where you would not naturally go.
Let Him become more than the Shepherd in a painting hanging on your wall.
The Bible is full of people whose lives would have destroyed their reputations if social media had existed.
Grace does not require a spotless résumé.
And Jesus Christ is still in the business of finding people whose stories look finished.
That is why shame does not get the final sentence.
Your failure does not get the final sentence.
Your addiction does not get the final sentence.
Your betrayal does not get the final sentence.
Your past does not get the final sentence.
But biblical grace is not Jesus editing your old life until it becomes socially acceptable.
It is Christ bringing sinners from death to life and teaching rescued sheep to follow their Shepherd.
Not to the approval of people.
The Shepherd who knows your name.
The Shepherd who sees your wounds.
The Shepherd who confronts your wandering.
The Shepherd who laid down His life.
And if your heart is whispering, “But you don't know what I've done”…
And the question has never been whether your sin is too ugly to shock Him.
The question is whether you will keep running from the only Shepherd who can save you.
But long after you close this article, remember this:
The Shepherd did not wait for the lost sheep to become worthy of being found—He came looking, laid down His life, rose again, and still calls the wandering home.
